summary: Describes the problem and the requirements for a framework to configure and manage IP Security policy. The framework should scale and be decentralized, covering how hosts and networks manage, discover, and negotiate policies on access, authentication, confidentiality, and integrity. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Computers need a way to agree on security rules without a person setting up each one. This memo lists what such a system must do.

questions: what are the requirements for ipsec policy management
what is policy discovery in ipsec
subtitle: What a framework for managing, discovering and negotiating IPsec security policy must provide.

tldr.problem: IPsec supports many uses, but nothing manages, negotiates or enforces the security policies under which security associations operate. This gets hard as networks grow and are run by different parties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out the problem space and lists what an IP Security Policy (IPSP) solution MUST include: a policy model, gateway discovery, a policy language, distributed policy, policy discovery, security association resolution and compliance checking.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It sets the target any IPSP framework has to meet without changing the IPsec standards.

facts.label: Changes to ESP, AH or IKE

today: RFC 3586 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It only states requirements and defines no protocol.

sections.title: Security Policy and IPsec
sections.content:
The RFC describes two uses of network-layer security. Security gateways, including firewalls, use IPsec at network edges for access control, confidentiality and authenticity, and VPN services. In end-to-end communication, hosts use IPsec for host-level access control and protection of traffic with their peers.

IPsec fits a wide range of schemes, but that range makes management hard as networks scale and different entities control different traffic. Key management protocols such as ISAKMP negotiate cryptographic parameters for IPsec security associations (SAs), but they do not provide a way to manage, negotiate or enforce the security policies under which SAs operate. IPSP is meant to fill that gap by managing IPsec policy, negotiating SA parameters between endpoints, and distributing authorization and policy information among hosts.
sections.eli5: IPsec is a strong lock, but someone still has to decide who gets a key and when. This memo is about that deciding.

sections.title: The Policy Problem Space
sections.content:
IPSP aims to be a scalable, decentralized framework. The RFC lists the traits of the problem:

  • IPSP hosts may be IPsec endpoints, security gateways, network management hubs, or a mix. That covers end-user computers, firewalls, VPN routers and servers.
  • Administration is heterogeneous and decentralized. Two hosts can set up an SA even when they share no policy or do not trust each other.
  • Acceptable SA parameters are often not known in advance and must be negotiated on the fly.
  • Some hosts follow policies not written in the IPSP language, so an IPSP specification is needed only for the parts that matter for interoperability.
  • It must scale, with remote control of many hosts and delegation of authority to different entities.
  • Its semantics must be well defined, and it must be secure, sound and comprehensible, with the security-critical parts small enough to verify. Ideally it works with formal methods.
sections.eli5: Different places have different rules, do not always trust each other, and need to work things out on the spot. The system has to cope with all that and stay understandable.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
An IPSP solution MUST include seven things: a policy model with well-defined semantics relating IPsec SAs to higher-level security policies; a gateway discovery mechanism; a well-specified policy language; a way to distribute responsibility for aspects of policy to different entities; a way to discover a host's policy; a mechanism to resolve the IPsec parameters to use between hosts under different policies (and decide whether any exist); and a mechanism to check compliance with a host's policy when SAs are created.

The mechanisms must not require protocol changes to ESP, AH or IKE. They must be independent of the SA-negotiation protocol, though they may assume certain functionality from it, so that future negotiation protocols stay compatible.
sections.eli5: There is a checklist of seven jobs the system must do, and it is not allowed to change the existing locks to do them.

sections.title: The Seven Components Explained
sections.content:
The policy model defines the meaning of IPsec policy and should be independent of how policy is distributed or discovered. Security gateway discovery finds which IPsec gateways lie between an initiator and its peer, may be invoked at any time to detect topology changes, and may carry information for other components.

The policy specification language is a common language for expressing the policies of hosts that must communicate. Vendor-specific policies would be translated into it when IPSP manages them. Distributed policy means all or part of a host's policy can be managed remotely, possibly by more than one entity.

Policy discovery gives two endpoints enough information to decide what SAs are possible, and a host need not reveal its entire policy, only enough to support SA resolution. SA resolution must find, in a computationally feasible way, SA parameters acceptable to both hosts.

Compliance checking verifies a proposed result against each host's local policy. The safety of the SAs created should depend only on this stage: even if resolution, which is likely complex, gives a wrong result, it should still not be possible to violate either host's policy.
sections.eli5: The parts are: a rulebook, a way to find the gate, a shared language for rules, a way for several people to look after rules, a way to peek at the other side's rules, a way to find a deal, and a final check that the deal breaks nobody's rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Status
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is brief. It says the document discusses high-level requirements for a policy framework and architecture for IPsec, and that a justification for each component is given. The IANA Considerations section says no action is required.

The document also includes a disclaimer that the views are those of the authors, not necessarily their employers, and it cites a Security Policy Protocol work in progress as an example of discovery that carries policy information.
sections.eli5: This memo does not build the lock. It describes what the lock system needs, so it adds no new security risks of its own to discuss.
